meta.title: SemHopQA: An Automated Pipeline for Generating Question-Answer Benchmarks for RAG System Evaluation in Spacecraft Operations

abstract: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in specialized fields remains a significant challenge, largely due to the lack of high-quality, domain-specific benchmarks. This is particularly acute in critical fields such as spacecraft operations, where rigorous assessment of system performance is essential. To address this, we present SemHopQA, an automated pipeline for generating single- and multi-hop question-answer (QA) datasets from unstructured spacecraft operations documentation. Our approach integrates Knowledge Graph (KG) construction with a random-walk traversal strategy to generate structurally grounded QA pairs based on explicit semantic paths. To ensure dataset integrity, we propose an automated LLM-asa-judge evaluation framework spanning three dimensions: clarity, grammar, and answerability. Experimental results show that SemHopQA competes directly with chunk-based generation frameworks like Hugging Face’s YourBench. While YourBench yields higher output volumes, our use of verified semantic paths produces significantly more answerable questions by minimizing reasoning hallucinations and chunking artifacts. This provides a reliable foundation for benchmarking RAG systems in documentation-heavy domains.

blocks.html: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly becoming important in our daily lives. Despite their state-of-the-art performance, they however still face persistent limitations: static knowledge cut-offs ("freezing"), the difficulty of integrating proprietary data without retraining, security risks regarding model weights, and a susceptibility to hallucinations. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a robust alternative to continuous retraining by providing models with context-specific external data [1]. However, adoption of RAG is hindered by complex validation requirements, which require the simultaneous evaluation of retrieval and generation accuracy [2] and the high costs associated with manual dataset curation [3].

These challenges are particularly acute in spacecraft operations, where procedures, technical documentation, and mission logs constitute a sensitive, specialized corpus that evolves continuously. Such environments demand the processing of extensive document collections characterized by intricate interdependencies. To address these constraints, recent literature advocates for the automated curation of synthetic, domain-tailored datasets [4]. This work contributes an integrated pipeline for the European Space Operations Centre (ESA/ESOC), merging knowledge graph construction, multi-hop question generation, and LLM-based evaluation into a cohesive framework optimized for technical documentation. By leveraging LLMs to generate question-answer (QA) benchmarks at scale, we provide a robust solution for the rigorous evaluation of RAG systems in mission-critical contexts [2, 5, 6].

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 details the proposed methodology. Evaluation setting and the results are presented and discussed in Section 3; Finally, we conclude in Section 4.

This section delineates the transformation pipeline designed for Knowledge Graph (KG) curation and multi-hop question generation. As illustrated in Figure 1, the workflow commences by normalizing raw documents into a unified format (Section 2.1) followed by a specialized preprocessing sequence to ensure data integrity. To facilitate semantic consistency, tabular data is restructured into coherent natural language (Section 2.2). Subsequently, both restructured tables and textual segments undergo a disambiguation phase to resolve coreferences and simplify complex linguistic structures. By ensuring semantic clarity prior to extraction, this targeted refinement enhances extraction precision and significantly reduces downstream computational overhead [7]. The resulting refined corpus serves as the basis for semantic triplet extraction to populate the KG, which provides the structural foundation for generating a synthetic multi-hop question-answering dataset (Section 2.4). Finally, the generation is coupled with an automated, LLM-based evaluation module (Section 2.5) to validate output quality.

Throughout this study, we used GPT-OSS-120B [8], deployed via a vLLM server to ensure high-throughput inference [9]. To ensure reliability and consistency of generation, the different prompts in the pipeline incorporate few-shot learning [10], chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning [11], and explicit task decomposition [12]. These prompting strategies were implemented using the LangChain [13] platform to enforce structured model outputs and maintain pipeline integrity [14].

blocks.html: The raw documents are first converted to Markdown format using PaddleOCR [15]. Subsequently, task-irrelevant document sections (e.g., copyright statements, figure tables) were removed. The documents are then sectioned into smaller portions, by section, subsection and then by size, creating chunks, facilitating data extraction [16]. To preserve semantic integrity, global context was extracted from each section via LLM prompting, providing necessary grounding for the chunks, leading to improved downstream results [17]. In this paper, we focus on tables and plain text; images are out of the scope of this work.

Mission operation documents contain both hierarchical and non-hierarchical tables. The former requires context-aware segmentation to preserve the logical flow and semantic integrity of dependent rows; conversely, the latter allows for more flexible partitioning as it is made up of in-dependent entries [18]. To handle these distinct structures, we utilized prompt engineering to contextually transform tabular data into natural language. This approach integrates LLM-generated table context to reduce the difficulty of the parsing task, thus improving accuracy and ensuring that the resulting text remains faithful to the original data structure [19].

To facilitate data extraction, both converted tables and plain-text chunks are first disambiguated by resolving pronouns and coreferences into explicit nouns. These refined sentences are then rewrote to a standardized subject–predicate–object (SPO) representation, reducing semantic complexity [20, 21].

The knowledge graph (KG) is constructed by extracting semantic triplets using an LLM-based approach adapted from recent methodologies [20, 21]. Following a formal (Subject)—[Predicate]→(Object) structure, subjects and objects are mapped as nodes, while predicates are cast as directed edges [22–24]. To maximize graph density and minimize redundancy, semantically equivalent entities are merged into unified nodes using semantic similarity and keyword matching. Furthermore, each node retains its source section as metadata, ensuring data provenance and enabling precise traceability during the questionevaluation phase. This structured representation supports efficient traversal and facilitates complex tasks such as multi-hop question generation.

Following KG construction, we implement a random walk traversal based on [25, 26] to generate multi-hop paths. Starting from a randomly selected node, the algorithm traverses outward, accumulating node and edge values until a predefined path depth, varying randomly between 2 and 4, is reached. These paths form the basis for complex multi-hop queries, which are subsequently transformed into natural language questions [26–28].

To generate question-answer (QA) pairs, we omit the final entity of a path and task the LLM with generating a question based on the preceding sequence. The omitted entity serves as the ground-truth answer. As a simple example, a traversal (Gaia,operated by,ESOC)→(ESOC,located in,Germany) produces the path Gaia→ESOC→Germany. By masking the last entity, the system generates the question: "What is the location of the operator of GAIA?" with the answer "Germany." This systematic approach creates benchmarks that require multi-step inference, supporting advanced RAG strategies such as chain-of-thought prompting and question decomposition [29, 30].

To ensure the integrity of the synthetically generated dataset, we implement a dedicated evaluation (that could serve as a QA pairs filtering in production) step to mitigate flaws such as ambiguity, grammatical errors, or unanswerability propagated during KG construction [31]. In high-stakes domains such as spacecraft operations, this validation is critical to establish the reliability of the system and to ensure that RAG benchmarking is not penalized by artifacts of the synthetic dataset generation process [32, 33]. Consequently, the generated question-answer pairs and their supporting passages are evaluated on three dimensions, Clarity, Grammar, and Answerability, using a qualitative 3-point scale (0–2). This ensures the dataset meets the fundamental criteria for RAG performance evaluation [34]. Clarity: Evaluates the unambiguity of subjects and objects within the question text [35].
• 0: Entities are vague pronouns (e.g., "it," "they").
• 1: Entities are non-specific or use demonstrative adjectives (e.g., "the algorithm").
• 2: Entities are precise and uniquely identifiable. Grammar: Assesses syntactic and linguistic correctness of the question generated [35].
• 0: Multiple errors hinder comprehension.
• 1: Minor flaws present but the question remains intelligible.
• 2: Grammatically correct with proper syntax and punctuation. Answerability: Measures the extent to which the source text fully supports the answer [34, 35].
• 0: Key entities are missing; answer cannot be inferred.
• 1: Partial information provided; requires moderate assumptions.
• 2: Source text fully encapsulates all required multihop steps.

We generated questions using a corpus of 75 ESA-internal mission manuals and 75 Gaia mission operational procedures, totaling 4,024 pages (2,784 and 1,240, respectively). To evaluate our proposed pipeline, we compared it against Hugging Face’s YourBench [36] on the same corpus. YourBench represents the dominant paradigm in automated benchmark curation: generating questions directly from retrieved document chunks and producing multi-hop items by jointly presenting multiple chunks. It serves as a well-matched baseline, differing from SemHopQA primarily in our core area of study, the explicit representation of reasoning paths prior to question generation.

The QA pairs from both pipelines were evaluated using the identical LLM-as-a-judge module (described in Section 2.5), ensuring that score variations stem entirely from the generation strategy rather than the evaluation protocol. To verify that the automated evaluator did not introduce bias, a random, unfiltered sample of 100 questions per system (stratified by hop count) was independently scored by two human annotators across the same three metrics, blind to the generation source. This produced paired human (H) and automated (AI) judgments for each system and metric.

Table 1 details the output volume for both pipelines. YourBench generated 1.84× more questions overall, with the disparity heavily concentrated in the multi-hop subset (6.84× more multi-hop items, compared to just 1.33× more single-hop items). Multi-hop questions comprise 34.2% of the YourBench dataset, but only 9.2% for SemHopQA.

This volume gap reflects a methodological divergence rather than an implementation deficiency. YourBench’s generation is largely unconstrained, processing any combination of chunks regardless of their actual semantic relation. In contrast, SemHopQA is strictly bounded by the generated knowledge graph; it only emits a multi-hop question when a random walk traverses verified edges. Chunks yielding sparse or disconnected subgraphs result in single-hop items or no output at all. While restricting generation to verified semantic paths lowers total volume, it guarantees that every question rests on a traceable evidence chain.

Table 2 breaks down these scores by hop count, revealing consistent trends within each dimension regardless of complexity. For Answerability, SemHopQA outperforms YourBench on both single-hop (∆= 0.292) and multi-hop items (∆= 0.332), with the performance gap widening for multi-hop questions. This aligns with the intuition that chunk-based generation degrades when a question requires multiple supporting facts. Conversely, for Grammar, YourBench retains a clear edge across single-hop (∆= −0.228) and multi-hop (∆= −0.372) items. This gap reflects the increased syntactic difficulty of formulating questions derived from discrete graph triplets compared to unstructured text. Clarity remains comparatively balanced, with a slight SemHopQA advantage on single-hop items (∆= 0.108) flipping to a marginal YourBench advantage on multi-hop items (∆= −0.065). Ultimately, multi-hop generation amplifies the baseline single-hop tendencies for each metric.

Table 3 presents the full score distributions and summary metrics on the manually annotated subsets. Across all dimensions, the automated LLM-as-a-judge demonstrates a uniquely conservative evaluation approach. As indicated by the high Conservative Scoring Rates, the AI evaluator acts as a strict quality gate, assigning scores that are equal to or harsher than human annotators in the vast majority of cases, thereby preventing the artificial inflation of the benchmark’s quality.

Clarity: Both frameworks perform robustly and are effectively indistinguishable. Human evaluators awarded the maximal score to 66.0% of SemHopQA questions against 60.5% for YourBench, confirming that both pipelines predominantly produce unambiguous, uniquely identifiable entities. Notably, approximately one third of the questions produced by either system fall in the intermediate band (score 1, non-specific or demonstrative entities). For SemHopQA, this residual under-specification is introduced downstream of the disambiguation stage, by entity merging: consolidating semantically equivalent nodes occasionally collapses distinct mission entities onto a generic label, restoring the very ambiguity that preprocessing had removed. Clarity is thus not a differentiator between the two paradigms but a shared limitation of LLM-based question realisation in a domain dense with near-homonymous identifiers. Furthermore, the automated judge validates this baseline reliably, exhibiting a Conservative Scoring Rate of 76.5% for SemHopQA and 75.5% for YourBench. Grammar: Both approaches generate highly articulate text, with human evaluators scoring 99.5% of SemHopQA items and 100% of YourBench items as comprehensible (score ≥1). However, YourBench holds an edge in perfect human-annotated scores (91.5% vs. 82.5%), benefiting from unconstrained generation over unstructured text. Crucially, as only 0.5% of SemHopQA questions were deemed incomprehensible by humans (score 0), the triplet-to-text conversion imposes only a minor cost to idiomatic fluency without compromising usability. In this dimension, the AI judge is exceptionally strict, scoring equal to or harsher than humans 93.0% of the time for SemHopQA and 92.0% for YourBench.

Answerability: The most critical divergence occurs here. Human evaluators found that 37.5% of YourBench questions were entirely unanswerable from the source text (score 0), compared to just 9.5% for SemHopQA. Conversely, 72.5% of SemHopQA questions are fully supported by the text (score 2), against only 25.0% for YourBench.

Manual inspection of the unanswerable YourBench items identifies three recurrent and mutually distinguishable error categories, all of which are consequences of generating questions from document chunks rather than from a factderived semantic path:

• Context-dependent artifacts (Chunk scaffolding references): The generated questions refer to the pipeline’s segmentation artifacts rather than the actual corpus content, invoking explicit chunk identifiers or ordinal positions (e.g., "in the second passage", "according to chunk 3"). This assumption generally fails in real-world deployments, as it inherently forces

• Reasoning hallucinations: Questions rely on hypothetical conditions, arbitrary values, or arithmetic conversions not explicitly supported by the retrieved text.
• Hallucinated entities and relationships: Questions presuppose entities or links absent from the source material, typically occurring when the model attempts to bridge semantically unrelated chunks.

blocks.html: These results highlight a fundamental trade-off between output volume, fluency, and factual grounding. While SemHopQA’s triplet-to-text conversion imposes a minor cost to perfect grammatical fluency, its structural knowledge graph constraints improve generated question answerability. The generation artifacts categorized in Table 4 demonstrate that YourBench’s performance gap is structural. Furthermore, while the Conservative Scoring Rate of the AI evaluator remains high across the board, the discrepancy between human and AI scores in Table 3 indicates that these specific artifacts frequently evade full detection by standard entailment-based automated judges, which underestimate the severity of the unanswerability. Because unanswerable items penalize the evaluated RAG system for flaws inherent to the benchmark itself, this makes factual grounding the primary criterion for dataset curation in critical fields like spacecraft operations.

This paper presented SemHopQA, a pipeline for the automated curation and evaluation of multi-hop QA pairs from unstructured spacecraft operations documents. By integrating Knowledge Graph (KG) construction, random walk navigation, and LLM-based evaluation, the proposed framework addresses the critical challenge of generating scalable, domain-specific datasets without the prohibitive costs of manual annotation. Our comparative evaluation illustrates a fundamental trade-off between throughput and factual grounding. Although unconstrained, chunk-based generation approaches yield higher output volumes, they introduce systematic errors, such as reasoning hallucinations and chunking artifacts, that frequently evade full detection by the LLM-as-a-judge evaluator.

By contrast, SemHopQA leverages a knowledge graph to ensure that every reasoning path is explicitly verified and supported by the source corpora. Although this structural constraint reduces the total yield and imposes a cost on grammar and clarity, it ensures significantly higher answerability. This provides a robust foundation for the rigorous benchmarking of RAG systems in critical fields such as spacecraft operations. While human-AI agreement varies across nuanced metrics like grammar, the high overall Conservative Scoring Rate confirms the automated evaluator’s utility as a reliable quality gate. Future work will focus on enhancing the grammatical fluency and clarity of SemHopQA’s outputs, as well as generating a broader diversity of questions by extending the pipeline to generate QA pairs for tool-augmented multi-agent systems.
